task_brief: Day 4 of "Algorithms, Efficiency, and Correctness" (unit 2, grade 10) is a build and test on correctness arguments and invariants and empirical timing and measurement. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 45–75 minutes. The unit is working toward: Compare searching and sorting approaches using complexity reasoning together with measured runtime evidence. Today's work contributes to that by handling correctness arguments and invariants and empirical timing and measurement at the application or project stage, against the unit's wider topics of searching algorithms, sorting algorithms, recursion and base cases, and complexity and growth rates. This session produces reviewable evidence toward the unit performance task.
primary_task: Build a working artifact for a stated need arising in the unit "Algorithms, Efficiency, and Correctness", built around what this session covers: correctness arguments and invariants and empirical timing and measurement. Write the requirements and the success conditions first, in testable form, before writing the artifact. Then implement it, run it against at least three cases — a normal case, a boundary case, and a case designed to break it — and log actual versus expected for each. Fix every failing case and re-run. Submit the artifact, the test log, and a short design note explaining one alternative you rejected and why. The activity_setup block below supplies the complete central input, exact specification, execution method, test cases, debugging target, and equal-credit manual simulation; use those exact materials rather than waiting for another handout, account, service, or tool. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about correctness arguments and invariants and empirical timing and measurement, and it belongs to "Algorithms, Efficiency, and Correctness", which also covers separate topics such as searching algorithms. Close out with this check before you stop: Show this session’s increment and name what remains before the task is complete. At grade 10 the bar is independent work that justifies its approach against a named alternative you considered and rejected, with the trade-off stated concretely.

central_input.title: Inline correctness arguments and invariants and empirical timing and measurement code case
central_input.purpose: Use this exact fictional case to investigate correctness arguments and invariants and empirical timing and measurement; no other file, model, dataset, or account is needed.

expected_behavior_and_specification: The algorithm must return the greatest member of a nonempty list; the supplied list must return 7.
The invariant is that best equals the greatest value examined so far, including when every value is negative.
The submitted explanation must connect the observed control flow or data state to correctness arguments and invariants and empirical timing and measurement, not merely state the final number.
The boundary test must be completed and its actual result compared explicitly with the expected result.

debugging_target.observed_failure: Starting best at 0 violates the stated invariant for an all-negative list, so the second test incorrectly returns 0.
debugging_target.target: Choose an initialization supported by the nonempty-list specification, state the loop invariant, and rerun all three tests.
debugging_target.passing_change: Initializing best from values[0] makes the invariant true before iteration; the tests return 7, -2, and 6.
debugging_target.scope_note: Diagnosing the state, control-flow, or data defect and connecting the repair to correctness arguments and invariants and empirical timing and measurement is the central evidence.
